Question: Which magazine had more previous names, Watercolor Artist or The General?

Evidence:
[d04p000] Dual naming
[d04s000] Dual naming is a policy for the naming of geographical landmarks, in which an official name is adopted that combines two previous names.
[d04s001] Usually, the context is a conflict over which of the two previous names is most appropriate.

[d05p000] Watercolor Artist
[d05s000] Watercolor Artist, formerly Watercolor Magic, is an American bi-monthly magazine that focuses on watermedia techniques, trends and artists.
[d05s001] As of June 2006, it had a print run of more than 90,000.

[d00p000] The General (magazine)
[d00s000] The General (1964–1998) was a bi-monthly periodical devoted to supporting Avalon Hill's line of wargames, with articles on game tactics, history, and industry news.
[d00s001] It was the first professionally produced wargaming magazine for the nascent cardboard and hex-map wargaming hobby.
[d00s002] Over the years the magazine was variously called "The Avalon Hill General", "Avalon Hill's General", "The General Magazine", or simply "General".

[d00p003] The General (magazine)
[d00s003] It was headquartered in Baltimore, Maryland.
[d00s004] With the sale of Avalon Hill to Hasbro in 1998 the magazine ceased.
[d00s005] Its unofficial heir was "Operations Magazine" published by Multi-Man Publishing to support the line of Avalon Hill games that remained in print, but that too went out of print in 2010, replaced by "Special Ops" magazine in 2011.

[d03p006] Maynard and Edith Hamlin Dixon House and Studio
[d03s006] Edith Dixon sold the home in 1963 to watercolor artist Milford Zornes, who occasionally used the studio.
[d03s007] The property is on the National Register of Historic Places and is open to the public.

Question: Alhambra and Tsuro are both examples of what type of game?

Evidence:
[d02p000] Tsuro
[d02s000] Tsuro is a tile-based board game designed by Tom McMurchie, originally published by WizKids and now published by Calliope Games.

[d04p003] Ayla-Axum amphorae
[d04s003] The Ayla-Axum/Aqaba amphora type has parallels from at least three terrestrial sites in Eritrea and Ethiopia: Aksum, where amphora sherds with gray fabric were found by the Deutsche Aksum Expedition (Zahn 1913: 208); Matara dating to the 4th through 7th centuries (Anfray 1990: 118); and Adulis (Paribeni 1907: 551) examples of which are on display in the National Museum in Asmara.
[d04s004] Other examples have been found at Berenike in Egypt, where the amphoras date firmly to an early 5th century context in what may be the best stratified examples (Hayes 1996: 159-61); from Aqaba in Jordan where many examples have been found, including their kilns; on The Shipwreck at Black Assarca Island, Eritrea (Pedersen 2008; Pedersen 2000); and in the Mediterranean such as on the late 6th-century shipwreck at Iskandil Burnu, Turkey, as well as in Spain and Carthage in strata datable from the mid-fourth to the sixth centuries (Keay 1986: 356, 358, 471).
[d04s005] The largest number (c. 500) came to light during excavations at Zafar/Yemen.

[d03p000] Artesonado
[d03s000] Artesonado is the name for a highly decorative coffered wooden ceiling in Spanish mudéjar architecture.
[d03s001] Examples are the ceilings in Throne room of the Aljafería (Zaragoza), Alhambra (Granada), the Chapterhouse of the Toledo Cathedral and the Royal Convent of Santa Clara (Tordesillas)
